item.content:encoded:
Florida's Department of Transportation has landed a three-hundred-fifty-six-million-dollar federal grant to overhaul rail crossing safety statewide. Combined with a hundred-million-dollar state investment, the four-hundred-fifty-six-million-dollar effort will upgrade more than nine-hundred rail crossings with new gates, lighting, signage, and pedestrian warning systems. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue calls it a transformational opportunity for rail safety. Crossings with the highest history of incidents will be prioritized first as the work rolls out.

Florida Power and Light now operates one-hundred-twenty solar energy centers across the state, making it the largest utility-scale solar portfolio in the country. The company says solar investments have saved customers more than one-point-three-billion dollars by avoiding fuel costs, with enough capacity now to power over one-and-a-half million homes. F-P-L has also added agrivoltaics projects at several sites, allowing land to be used for both solar production and cattle grazing at the same time.

item.title: Mayor Reeves Reacts to Re-Election Win, Curfew Failure, Veterans Park Restrooms and More
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Mayor D.C. Reeves joined Pensacola's Morning News Wednesday morning fresh off his re-election victory — calling in from school drop-off where he and daughter Caroline were celebrating after a long night of sign-waving at Bayview Park and a victory party. The mayor earned 53 percent of the vote in Tuesday's primary…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Mayor D.C. Reeves joined Pensacola's Morning News Wednesday morning fresh off his re-election victory — calling in from school drop-off where he and daughter Caroline were celebrating after a long night of sign-waving at Bayview Park and a victory party. The mayor earned 53 percent of the vote in Tuesday's primary — defeating five challengers without a runoff and securing a second term without a November race.


The Re-Election

Reeves says the margin told him something important about how Pensacola residents actually feel about their city — and says it is very different from the picture painted on social media. He says decisions are not made in Facebook comment sections — they are made in living rooms when parents are FaceTiming their kids in college and thinking about whether Pensacola is a place they want to come home to. He says the vote tells him the city is going in the right direction and that residents want to keep pushing forward — not tear things down. He was quick to say he knows he can be a better mayor and that the city can always improve — but says acknowledging imperfection and declaring the city broken are two very different things. Reeves first won the mayor's race in 2022 at 38 years old, also without a runoff. The final results — Reeves 53 percent, Alicia Trawick 21 percent, Ann Hill 10 percent, Jermaine Williams 8 percent, Jasmine Brown 4 percent, Eric Shorter 3 percent.


Juvenile Curfew — Coming Back in September

Reeves was visibly frustrated about the juvenile curfew ordinance's failure at city council last week — and said the process leading up to the vote was more troubling than the vote itself. He says his team spent almost two weeks preparing the proposal and that every council member who showed up with last-minute objections had the same two weeks to raise those concerns privately and did not. He called that disrespectful to Police Chief Eric Winstrom — who has been the strongest advocate for the tool — and to the city attorney's office that did the legal work. He singled out Councilman Charles Bare for sending a written opposition document before even hearing from the chief — saying Bare burned the boat before the conversation started. Reeves also addressed the broader pattern of council decisions being driven by Facebook reaction rather than actual engagement with the substance of what is being proposed — saying there is a meaningful difference between showing up at a meeting and actually reading the ordinance you are opposing. The curfew ordinance will be brought back before city council in September. Reeves says he remains open to any conversation about how to improve it — before the meeting, not at the podium.


Land Development Code and Trees

The land development code overhaul that recently cleared city council will be followed up with additional protections for heritage oaks and southern live oaks. Reeves says he and Councilman Jared Moore are developing those additional specifications — which will come as a separate item rather than delay the broader LDC rewrite that had already begun. He says the goal is to make sure the trees the community loves most are genuinely protected going forward.


Veterans Memorial Park Restrooms

The two-bathroom prefab facility at Veterans Memorial Park has been approved by city council and is on track for completion by early 2027. Reeves defended the decision against critics who wanted four bathrooms — noting that only one park in the city's 95-park portfolio has two bathrooms outside of parks with community centers. He also pointed out that even four bathrooms would not be sufficient for major events like Veterans Day and Memorial Day when portable facilities are still needed regardless of what is permanently installed. He says the flood zone restrictions on the site limited options and that the city made the right call given the constraints. He says after 12 years of discussion he is simply looking forward to getting it done.


Second Term Priorities

Reeves says his second term will be defined by getting major projects already in motion across the finish line — specifically Birdon shipbuilding at the port, the $110 million airport terminal expansion, the Reverb development at Maritime Park, the Baptist Hospital site redevelopment, and a possible inland port at the Super Fun site that he says could significantly expand the port's economic development capacity. He says the city is going on offense and does not plan to slow down.

item.title: Primary results for Northwest Florida
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Santa Rosa County Jeff Ates won the Republican primary for Santa Rosa County Commission District 2 , finishing first in a six-candidate field. Ates received 6,073 votes, or 26.40% of the 23,003 ballots cast. He finished 1,592 votes ahead of former Milton City Councilman Jeff Snow, who received 4,481 votes. Reni “Renee” Johnmeyer finished third…
item.content:encoded:
Santa Rosa County

Jeff Ates won the Republican primary for Santa Rosa County Commission District 2, finishing first in a six-candidate field. Ates received 6,073 votes, or 26.40% of the 23,003 ballots cast. He finished 1,592 votes ahead of former Milton City Councilman Jeff Snow, who received 4,481 votes.

Reni “Renee” Johnmeyer finished third with 3,827 votes, followed by Erin Nisewonger with 3,589. Incumbent Kerry Smith finished fifth with 3,425 votes, while RC Pittman received 1,608. Ates will face write-in candidate John Williams in the November 3 election.

Dean Light defeated incumbent Ray Eddington in the Santa Rosa County Commission District 4 race. With all 41 precincts reporting, Light received 14,421 votes, or 51.13%, compared with Eddington's 13,783 votes, or 48.87%. The result continues a trend dating to the 2011 redistricting: according to the information provided, no District 4 incumbent has won reelection since the district lines were redrawn because of growth in southern Santa Rosa County.

Holley-Navarre Fire District voters approved the district's first fee increase in 10 years. The referendum passed 56.71% to 43.29%, with 3,682 voters supporting it and 2,811 opposed. The increase will raise the annual residential fee from about $162 to $231 for homes up to 2,300 square feet, an increase of roughly $5.70 per month.


Escambia and Santa Rosa state races

Jon Fay won the Republican nomination for Florida House District 2. The retired Navy flight officer and former Blue Angels executive officer received 14,642 votes across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties, compared with 4,190 for Trei McMullen. Fay won approximately 79% of the vote in Escambia County and 75% in Santa Rosa County.

Fay will face Democratic nominee Johnny Austin Thompson in November. Thompson is a 25-year-old Washington High School graduate and current Harvard Law student.

Escambia County District 2 Commissioner Mike Kohler also won his Republican primary, defeating Glenn Dorsey. With all but one district reporting, Kohler had 2,998 votes, or 62.41%, while Dorsey had 1,806 votes, or 37.59%.


Escambia County School Board

All three Escambia County School Board incumbents who faced challengers won reelection.

Kevin Adams defeated Erin Toler in District 1 and will serve a third term. Adams had 6,638 votes, or 60.92%, compared with Toler's 4,259 votes, or 39.08%, with 12 of 13 precincts reporting.

In District 2, three-term incumbent Paul Fetsko defeated Gerald Washington. Fetsko had 5,024 votes, or 66.29%, compared with Washington's 2,555 votes, or 33.71%, with 15 of 16 precincts reporting.

David Williams also won a second term in District 3, defeating newcomer Isaac Williams.

Because the school board races are nonpartisan and only two candidates were on the ballot in each race, the primary winners were elected outright rather than advancing to a November runoff.

Voters also overwhelmingly approved a referendum that will restore an elected school superintendent in Escambia County. With 75 of 80 precincts reporting, 36,889 voters, or 71.22%, supported the measure, while 14,905, or 28.78%, opposed it.


Pensacola

Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves won reelection outright. With all 20 precincts reporting, Reeves received 53.45% of the vote. Under the city's charter, a candidate who receives more than 50% in the August election wins the office without a runoff.


Statewide and congressional races

Byron Donalds won the Republican nomination for Florida governor, defeating Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, James Fishback and former House Speaker Paul Renner. With nearly 1.4 million votes counted, Donalds had 49%, followed by Collins with 25%, Fishback with 10% and Renner with 8%. The Associated Press called the race shortly after 8 p.m. Eastern.

Congressman Jimmy Patronis won the Republican primary for Florida's 1st Congressional District, with the Associated Press calling the race at 7:17 p.m. Central.

item.title: Florida Primary Election Results: Moody, Donalds Lead Republican Races
item.dc:creator: Robert Rees
item.description: Florida voters cast ballots Tuesday in the state's primary election, determining nominees for U.S. Senate, U.S. House of Representatives, Florida Governor, and numerous state races ahead of November's general election. On the Republican side for governor, Byron Donalds secured a commanding lead with 798,921 votes, or 47.9 percent of the GOP…
item.content:encoded:
Florida voters cast ballots Tuesday in the state's primary election, determining nominees for U.S. Senate, U.S. House of Representatives, Florida Governor, and numerous state races ahead of November's general election.

On the Republican side for governor, Byron Donalds secured a commanding lead with 798,921 votes, or 47.9 percent of the GOP primary vote. Jay Collins finished second with 419,013 votes representing 25.12 percent of the field.

Democrats rallied behind a unified ticket, with the David Jolly and Gwen Graham partnership capturing 746,788 votes, or 61.02 percent of the Democratic primary for governor. The tandem significantly outpaced rival Dayna Marie Foster, who received 184,550 votes.

In the U.S. Senate race, Republican Ashley Moody dominated her primary with a decisive victory, earning 1,296,258 votes for 79.57 percent of GOP voters. Her closest competitor, Chris Gleason, garnered only 223,758 votes.

On the Democratic side, Angie Nixon prevailed with 687,075 votes, representing 55.94 percent of the primary electorate. Alex Vindman came in second with 541,123 votes, or 44.06 percent.

In congressional races across Florida's districts, Republican Jimmy Patronis dominated District 1 with 61,918 votes, claiming 71.19 percent of that primary. In District 5, Republican John H. Rutherford secured victory with 52,977 votes for 67.7 percent of the Republican primary.

Democratic congressional nominee races saw various winners emerge across the state's districts, with candidates like Leela Gray capturing 65.14 percent of the District 13 Democratic primary.

Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time Tuesday, with results released shortly thereafter through the Associated Press. The primary elections set the stage for competitive general election matchups this November across multiple statewide and congressional races that will shape Florida's political landscape.

item.title: Escambia Sheriff Covers Showalter Park Homicide, Flock Camera Debate, Ferry Pass Murder and More
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Escambia County, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons joined Pensacola's Morning News on election day Tuesday with an update on several recent incidents, leading with a Showalter Park homicide that started as an organized fight and ended with one man dead and another shot, and delivering his most comprehensive defense yet of…
item.content:encoded:
Escambia County, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons joined Pensacola's Morning News on election day Tuesday with an update on several recent incidents, leading with a Showalter Park homicide that started as an organized fight and ended with one man dead and another shot, and delivering his most comprehensive defense yet of Flock license plate reader cameras.


Showalter Park Homicide

Two men arranged to meet at Showalter Park to fight over a situation involving a woman — with seven or eight people gathering to watch. After the fight concluded a bystander approached one of the combatants — who had a handgun in his waistband — and attempted to rob him of the weapon at gunpoint. The robber opened fire striking the man multiple times in the torso and killing him. A second person was shot in the leg with non-life-threatening injuries. Simmons says the group organized the fight online — meaning most of them were recording video — and says investigators have already zeroed in on a suspect while working to establish probable cause. He says cooperation from witnesses is coming in and investigators are making progress.


Ferry Pass Domestic Homicide

A welfare check in Ferry Pass led to the discovery of a man shot and killed while lying in his bed. Simmons says the victim's parents — who had not heard from their son in some time — became suspicious and contacted law enforcement. The case is domestic in nature involving two long-term roommates. Simmons declined to provide additional details citing victim protection requirements.


Armed Robbery at Plasma Center

Two women taking a break behind a plasma center were robbed at gunpoint by a man who took jewelry and other items. The suspect was arrested — and had reportedly returned to his job at a dealership after the robbery. Some of the stolen property was recovered.


Flock Camera Debate — Simmons's Most Comprehensive Defense Yet

Simmons engaged in a lengthy and substantive debate with Andrew McKay on Flock license plate reader cameras — delivering what may be his most forceful defense of the technology to date. His core argument is that there is no expectation of privacy on public roadways — a principle already established by the Supreme Court and exercised every time a deputy manually runs a plate while driving. He cited Thomas Jefferson's observation that laws and institutions must evolve alongside human progress — saying Jefferson could not have envisioned license plate readers but would have understood the principle. Simmons said the Flock cameras are the most valuable law enforcement tool he has seen in 40 years of law enforcement — more valuable in his view than fingerprints or DNA. He said if forced to choose one of the three he would take license plate readers without hesitation. He says statewide there would be hundreds if not thousands of serious criminals still on the streets without them — and finds it peculiar that critics single out this particular technology while accepting every other form of modern surveillance. He also noted that Flock recently announced reforms that ECSO already had in place.


Rivera Sign Complaint

The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is reviewing a complaint filed by a Mr. McMillan against Ronnie Rivera — an Escambia County Sheriff's Office employee and experienced local campaign operative — related to a political sign dispute near an early voting location. Sheriff Chip Simmons says his office received both a criminal complaint and an internal policy complaint tied to Rivera's employment with the agency — and referred both to FDLE rather than handle them in-house given the conflict of interest. Simmons says the statute in question deals with business and permitted signs rather than political signs specifically — and notes as a former candidate himself that sign disputes near busy polling locations happen hundreds of times every election cycle. FDLE is handling the criminal review.

item.title: Congressman Jimmy Patronis: Sewing Box Update, USS Lincoln, South Korea, VA Advocacy and More
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Northwest Florida Congressman Jimmy Patronis joined Pensacola's Morning News today with an update on several issues — covering the latest on the Sewing Box Blue Angels contract fight, weighing in on the USS Abraham Lincoln extended deployment, and sharing a personal story about advocating for a wheelchair-bound…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Northwest Florida Congressman Jimmy Patronis joined Pensacola's Morning News today with an update on several issues — covering the latest on the Sewing Box Blue Angels contract fight, weighing in on the USS Abraham Lincoln extended deployment, and sharing a personal story about advocating for a wheelchair-bound veteran stuck in a VA dispute.


Sewing Box Blue Angels Contract

Patronis says his office sent a formal letter to the Navy asking for a full accounting of the procurement process — including public notice periods, deadlines, and timelines. He says the letter also asked about options to bring The Sewing Box in as a subcontractor on the existing contract and requested the expiration date of the current award so the shop can be positioned for the next procurement cycle. Patronis says if the Navy followed the letter of the law the most viable path for owner Candy White-Hirsch may be a bid protest — a formal legal challenge to the procurement. He says he would be shocked if a response doesn't come within 48 hours to a week.


USS Abraham Lincoln

Patronis — who served aboard the USS Harry S. Truman — says the situation aboard the Abraham Lincoln needs to be understood in context. He says working ships run around the clock and that 200-plus days at sea without seeing loved ones creates genuine psychological pressure — particularly for the very young men and women who make up most of the crew. He noted that fresh fruit and produce have to be flown in and that basic comforts are harder to come by than people on shore realize. He also pointed out that the Lincoln's sailors are flying combat missions in an aggressor role that this generation of naval aviators has not experienced before — a genuinely new set of emotions and pressures on top of an already demanding deployment. He noted that reenlistment rates aboard the Lincoln are reportedly higher than most other vessels — a data point he says complicates the narrative around morale.


South Korea and Allied Support

Patronis said he has been blown away by how few American allies have stepped up to support operations against Iran — and said President Trump has largely been going it alone. He acknowledged South Korea has a new government still trying to establish stability at home but said the U.S. has a massive human investment in that country and that some reciprocity in shared security burdens would be reasonable to expect.


Democratic Socialists

Patronis warned listeners not to dismiss the Democratic Socialists of America as a fringe movement — saying their charismatic leaders are resonating with younger voters and that they are already showing up at school boards, county commissions, and city councils across the country. He says the Democrat Party welcomed them into a big tent and is now being eaten from the inside out — with DSA-aligned candidates taking out incumbent Democrats in primaries across the nation. He says the answer is governance that uses policy and rules to push back — not dismissal.


VA Benefits Advocacy

Patronis shared a personal story about a veteran he is actively working to help — a young man who is wheelchair-bound after a 30-foot fall but is rated at only 30 percent disability because the VA is characterizing some of his injuries as preexisting. Patronis says he has been making calls personally in the last 24 hours to move the case forward. He says his office handles hundreds of VA cases every month and says navigating the system on behalf of veterans who cannot do it alone is one of the most meaningful parts of the job. Anyone who needs help with a VA claim can contact Congressman Patronis's office directly.

item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- South Florida businesses are reportedly scrambling to fill staffing gaps after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for Haitian immigrants in late July. According to a WSJ report, home-care agencies, nursing homes, and restaurants across the state are reporting losing longtime employees overnight, with some organizations shutting down entirely. Florida is home to nearly half the roughly three-hundred-fifty-thousand Haitian TPS holders nationwide, with about ninety-three-thousand in the state's workforce. Supporters of the policy argue it restores TPS to its original temporary purpose and opens jobs for other workers, while opponents say the change is pulling essential caregivers and staff out of the economy.

item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Civil claims against former Escambia County Deputy Greg Nesmith have been dropped, though his criminal case remains pending. Nesmith faces two counts of vehicular homicide after fatally hitting two Alabama teenagers crossing Perdido Key Drive last July while off duty. His attorneys say conflicting details between two official crash reports may have influenced the felony charges against him, and they've requested a hearing to examine how the investigation was handled. Nesmith has pleaded not guilty and is due back in court February seventeenth.

item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Polls are open today in Escambia County from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. — and Supervisor of Elections Robert Bender joined Pensacola Morning News this morning with everything voters need to know before they head out. Everyone Has Something to Vote On Every registered voter in Escambia County has a ballot today. The…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Polls are open today in Escambia County from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. — and Supervisor of Elections Robert Bender joined Pensacola Morning News this morning with everything voters need to know before they head out.


Everyone Has Something to Vote On

Every registered voter in Escambia County has a ballot today. The countywide referendum on whether to make the school superintendent an appointed rather than elected position appears on every ballot regardless of party. Three nonpartisan school board races in Districts 1, 2, and 3 are also on the ballot — with only two candidates in each race meaning all three new school board members will be known tonight. The six-candidate mayor's race is on the ballot for all City of Pensacola residents — and if any candidate clears 50 percent today there will be no November mayoral election.


Partisan races include U.S. Senate, governor and lieutenant governor, CFO, commissioner of agriculture, and for Republicans a congressional race and a county commission District 2 race. Some ballots ran to three columns.


Governor and Lieutenant Governor — Vote for One

Bender says this is generating significant confusion at the polls. The race is called governor and lieutenant governor — but voters should only select one candidate. On the Republican side no candidates submitted a lieutenant governor — so only governor names appear. On the Democratic side David Jolly selected Gwen Graham as his running mate — her name appears under his slightly offset. Calls are coming in asking where her oval is. She does not have one — she is on the same ticket as Jolly. Vote for one. If a voter accidentally selects two the tabulator will flag it and give them an opportunity to correct it before the ballot is cast.


Your Polling Place

Today you must go to your home precinct — early vote sites are closed. If your polling location changed you were sent a new voter information card. A-frame signs are posted at all changed locations to direct you to your correct precinct. Southwest Library is closed today — it was an early vote site only. New temporary locations include the Fricker Center at the main library downtown and Precinct 70 at the Gathering Place at Pensacola Christian College near I-10.


Lost Your Mail-In Ballot

Just show up and vote in person. The system updates in real time — if your mail-in ballot has not been scanned you will receive a regular ballot at your precinct. If you want to drop off a completed mail-in ballot the only option today is the Supervisor of Elections office downtown — no other locations accept them on election day. All ballots must be in Bender's possession by 7 p.m. tonight. Mailing a ballot today is possible but a gamble — postmark does not count in a primary.


Voting Machines

Bender addressed the persistent question directly — voting machines are not sitting connected to the internet. Results are transmitted via a closed network system initiated by election workers after polls close — a 30-second upload. Bender expects the majority of results to be posted between 7:35 and 7:45 tonight. An independent audit will run all ballots through again in the next two days to confirm totals.


One More Thing

No firearms at polling places. It is one of the designated prohibited locations under Florida law — bringing a weapon to the polls is a felony charge. Leave it at home.

Questions can be directed to the Supervisor of Elections office at 850-595-3900 or escambiavotes.gov. Polls close at 7 p.m.
